Yellow-bellied marmots (Marmota flaviventris) exhibit a life history pattern typical of large, hibernating sciurids, with a relatively slow pace of life. Neonates emerge into the world at a remarkably small body size, with field records indicating a wet weight at birth of 33.8 grams [Wwb = 33.8 grams]. This modest initial mass underscores the altricial state of the newborn pups, which are entirely dependent on maternal care and thermoregulation within the subterranean natal burrow. The developmental trajectory from this fragile neonatal stage toward weaning unfolds over a period of 33 days since birth [tx = 33 days since birth], a duration that reflects the rich lipid content of marmot milk and the concentrated energy transfer from the mother at a temperature of 36.5 °C [T = 36.5 °C]. During this suckling period, the pups experience an accelerated phase of mass gain as they transition from complete dependence to nutritional emancipation, reaching a wet weight at weaning of 479 grams [Wwx = 479 grams] by the time of first emergence from the burrow.

The timing of reproductive events in Marmota flaviventris is tightly constrained by the short active season at high elevations. Gestation, which occurs shortly after the female emerges from hibernation in early spring, has a duration of approximately 30 days [tg = approximately 30 days] when measured under the core body temperature typical of euthermic marmots (36.5 °C [T = 36.5 °C]). This relatively brief gestation is followed by the protracted lactational period, culminating in weaning at 33 days [tx = 33 days], a value that is consistent across most populations occupying the Sierra Nevada and Rocky Mountain ranges at a temperature of 36.5 °C [T = 36.5 °C]. Following weaning, the young marmots continue to grow rapidly throughout their first summer of life. They reach the pubertal threshold after spending their first hibernation, with time since birth at puberty estimated at 730 days after birth [tp = 730 days after birth], meaning individuals typically become reproductively competent in their second spring after birth, a pattern that underscores the importance of accruing sufficient body mass to survive the prolonged winter fast at a temperature of 36.5 °C [T = 36.5 °C].

Females of this species are capable of achieving an impressive annual reproductive output given the brevity of the active season. Detailed field studies conducted at the Rocky Mountain Biological Laboratory in Colorado indicate that a typical female produces a single litter each year [F_R_i = a single litter each year], containing approximately 4 pups per litter [N_R_i = containing approximately 4 pups per litter]. This annual reproductive rate is relatively conservative compared to smaller rodents, reflecting the marmot's bet-hedging strategy in an unpredictable alpine environment. The ultimate wet weight attained by adult females, measured during the peak of the post-hibernation foraging period, reaches approximately 3500 grams [Wwi = approximately 3500 grams], though individuals can occasionally exceed 5 kilograms in particularly productive years. This substantial adult body mass is a key determinant of hibernation survival and future reproductive success, as females must accumulate sufficient fat reserves to sustain themselves and their developing litter through the long winter dormancy.

The maximum lifespan observed in wild populations of Yellow-bellied marmots is considerable for a rodent of this size. At the standard body temperature of 36.5 °C [T = 36.5 °C], which represents the normothermic active state, the maximum longevity has been recorded at approximately 21.2 years [am = approximately 21.2 years], with several marked individuals documented to have persisted for over two decades in intensively monitored colonies. This extended lifespan, coupled with the relatively delayed onset of reproduction, places marmots at the slow end of the life-history continuum among North American ground squirrels. The longevity is thought to be facilitated by their protective burrow systems, social vigilance against predators, and the metabolic savings accrued during deep hibernation, which may reduce cumulative oxidative damage over the animal's lifetime. Comparisons with congeneric species such as the woodchuck (Marmota monax) and the Olympic marmot (Marmota olympus) suggest that these longevity estimates are consistent with the broader marmot lineage.

The interplay between maternal body condition, hibernation duration, and spring phenology creates substantial interannual variation in breeding success among Yellow-bellied marmots, with younger or smaller females often skipping reproduction entirely. At the active euthermic core body temperature of 36.5 °C [T = 36.5 °C], the maximum achievable reproductive output translates to approximately 4 pups per litter [N_R_i = approximately 4 pups per litter] at a frequency of approximately 1.1 litters per year [F_R_i = approximately 1.1 litters per year], underscoring that not all females breed annually, particularly following harsh winters. Such flexibility in reproductive scheduling is a hallmark of long-lived, iteroparous mammals inhabiting seasonally severe environments, allowing individuals to prioritize survival over current-year offspring production when conditions are suboptimal, a strategy that aligns with the substantial adult body mass (3500 grams) [Wwi = 3500 grams] needed to survive the prolonged winter fast.
